text: John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, and polymath who made foundational contributions across multiple disciplines. Born in Budapest in 1903, he was a child prodigy, excelling in mathematics and languages from an early age. He earned a doctorate in mathematics and later became a leading figure in set theory, where he introduced the axiom of foundation and the concept of classes, and developed the modern definition of ordinal numbers. His work in ergodic theory, measure theory, and functional analysis laid the groundwork for modern mathematical physics and quantum mechanics. He established the Dirac–von Neumann axioms for quantum mechanics, introducing the density matrix and von Neumann entropy, which are fundamental in quantum information theory. In computer science, he is credited with the "von Neumann architecture," which stores both data and programs in the same memory space, forming the basis of modern computing. He also pioneered the Monte Carlo method and developed algorithms like merge sort. In economics, he founded game theory with Oskar Morgenstern, proving the minimax theorem, and developed a model of an expanding economy using fixed-point theorems. His work in the Manhattan Project, including the design of explosive lenses for the hydrogen bomb, was instrumental in nuclear weapons development. A key advocate for the use of computers in scientific research, he helped establish computational methods for fluid dynamics and weather prediction. Von Neumann was known for his exceptional intellect, intuitive problem-solving, and eidetic memory, and he remained active in both academic and military affairs throughout his life. He died in 1957 at age 53 from cancer and is widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential scientists of the 20th century.
